mcqs.question: A service handles thousands of mostly-idle connections waiting on slow network I/O, running on a single CPU core using an event loop. Is this system concurrent, parallel, both, or neither?
options: Concurrent but not parallel — many tasks are in progress over overlapping time, but only one instruction executes at any single instant on one core
Parallel but not concurrent, since the event loop schedules tasks independently
Both concurrent and parallel, since thousands of connections are active
Neither, since a single core cannot support true concurrency
mcqs.explanation: Concurrency describes overlapping logical progress; parallelism requires simultaneous execution, which needs multiple cores. A single-core event loop interleaves many tasks over time — genuinely concurrent — but never executes more than one instruction at once, so it is not parallel.

mcqs.question: A computation is 90% parallelizable and 10% inherently serial. Using Amdahl's Law, roughly what speedup do you get going from 10 processors to 1,000 processors?
options: Speedup goes from about 5.3x to about 9.9x — most of the remaining gain toward the 10x ceiling is already captured by 10 processors, and 1,000 barely improves on it
Speedup goes from 10x to 1,000x, scaling linearly with processor count
Speedup goes from 5.3x to 100x, since more processors always multiply speedup proportionally
Speedup stays exactly the same regardless of processor count once any serial fraction exists
mcqs.explanation: With P=0.9, the ceiling is 1/(1-0.9)=10x. At N=10, speedup is 1/(0.1+0.9/10)=5.3x; at N=1,000, it's 1/(0.1+0.9/1000)≈9.9x — the curve flattens hard well before infinite processors, so massively over-provisioning cores yields rapidly diminishing returns once a serial fraction exists.

mcqs.question: A lock protects a critical section that runs on every request under high concurrency. Why does this specific lock matter far more for performance than a lock protecting a rarely-called, tiny critical section?
options: Locks always have identical performance cost regardless of how often they're acquired or how long they're held

Contention severity scales with both critical-section size (time held) and acquisition frequency — a lock held often and for longer under high concurrency serializes far more total work than one rarely touched
Only locks on database connections meaningfully affect performance
The lock's cost depends only on the number of lines of code inside the critical section, not on how often it's called
mcqs.explanation: Lock contention cost is a function of both how long the critical section holds the lock and how often threads want it — a lock on a hot path under high concurrency effectively serializes a large fraction of total work, while the same lock on a rarely-called path costs almost nothing. Both factors matter, not just code size.

mcqs.question: A shared counter is incremented extremely frequently by many threads, and an exact, always-up-to-the-instant total is not required — an approximate total summed occasionally is fine. Which contention-reduction technique fits this specific case best?
options: Sharding — splitting the counter into N independent per-thread or per-bucket counters that are summed only when a total is actually needed, so most increments never contend at all
A single global lock around the counter, since correctness requires serializing every increment
Immutability, since the counter's value should never change
False-sharing padding, since that is the only technique that applies to counters
mcqs.explanation: Sharding is exactly suited to a workload that tolerates an approximate, eventually-summed total: most increments hit independent shards and never contend, while only the occasional read pays a cost proportional to shard count. Immutability doesn't fit since the value does change; a single lock reintroduces the exact contention being avoided.

mcqs.question: Two threads each update their own separate, unshared counter — no lock anywhere in the code — yet throughput scales terribly as more threads are added. What is the most likely cause?
options: The counters must actually be shared somewhere, since unshared variables cannot cause contention
This is expected behavior and indicates the workload is fundamentally not parallelizable
False sharing — the two counters happen to sit on the same CPU cache line, so a write to one invalidates the cache line for the other core even though there is no logical dependency between them
The compiler is failing to inline the counter increment operations
mcqs.explanation: False sharing occurs when logically independent variables share a cache line — a write from one thread invalidates the whole line for other cores, creating throughput-killing contention with no lock or shared data anywhere in the code. Padding the variables so each occupies its own cache line is the standard fix.

mcqs.question: CPU utilization looks low under load, so a team doubles the thread pool size, but throughput drops further. What diagnostic step would have predicted this outcome?
options: Checking whether low CPU utilization is due to genuine idleness or to threads blocked waiting on a shared lock — the latter means more threads add contenders to the same bottleneck rather than new capacity
Measuring the total number of lines of code in the critical section
Increasing the CPU clock speed instead of the thread count
Checking whether the workload is CPU-bound by counting the number of physical cores available
mcqs.explanation: Low CPU utilization under load is ambiguous — it can mean genuine idle capacity (more threads help) or threads blocked waiting on a lock (more threads just lengthen the wait queue, worsening context-switch overhead without adding real capacity). Off-CPU/lock-wait profiling distinguishes the two before committing to 'add more threads.'
